content.text: The text first recounts Thomas Paine’s return from France to America in 1802, his stays in Baltimore, Washington, Bordentown, New York, Stonington, and New Rochelle, and his political, religious, mechanical, and humanitarian work. It describes his advocacy for Louisiana’s purchase, opposition to slavery, defense of Jefferson, persecution for deism, poverty, illness, disputed reputation, and death in Greenwich, New York, in 1809. His friends buried him at his New Rochelle farm; later, William Cobbett exhumed his bones and took them to England. Appendices preserve memoirs, letters, portraits, and recollections emphasizing Paine’s intellect, generosity, sobriety, and enduring influence. The text then shifts to fiction: Allan Cameron and Mandy return home after aiding an injured Piegan boy, encounter Chief Onawata, and learn Cameron must pursue him amid fears of an Indian uprising.
